title: Sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi: the first of the five ‘brahma’ mantras
theme: Refuge in Sadyojāta, the first of the five faces of Śiva, with the plea to be led beyond birth after birth.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: the western face of the five-faced Lord, «सद्योजातनामकं यत्पश्चिमवक्त्रं तद्रूपं परमेश्वरं प्रपद्यामि प्राप्नोमि»

words.meaning: I go to [for refuge], I approach

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «तत्तज्जन्मनिर्मितं» — on account of each birth

words.role: negates the verb (construed with bhave bhave)

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «जन्मातिलङ्घननिमित्तं» — for passing beyond birth
The anonymous commentator glosses «प्रेरय» — impel; Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara read bhajasva

words.meaning: to the one who lifts out of becoming

sandhi.rule: sadyojātam + prapadyāmi → sadyojātaṃ prapadyāmi: m becomes anusvāra (P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः)).

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: namaḥ + namaḥ → namo namaḥ: -aḥ becomes -o before a voiced sound.
na + atibhave → nātibhave: like vowels merge long (P. 6.1.101 (अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः)).

samasa.meaning: born at once, on the instant
the one who raises [one] out of becoming

morphology.note: An āmreḍita: the locative repeated means ‘in each birth’; written as one word, as Vedic repetitions are.
As printed, a middle imperative of √bhū, which is rare. Sāyaṇa’s and Bhāskara’s texts read bhajasva (√bhaj, ‘resort to, assign’); see flags.
The first member is the adverb sadyas, ‘at once’; its final s becomes o before the voiced j.

translation.literal: I go [for refuge] to Sadyojāta; to Sadyojāta truly homage, homage. In birth after birth — not [so]; in what is beyond birth bring me. To the one who lifts [us] out of becoming, homage.
translation.readable: I take refuge in Sadyojāta; homage, homage to Sadyojāta. Do not keep me in birth after birth; lead me beyond birth. Homage to the one who raises us out of becoming.

anvaya: सद्योजातम् प्रपद्यामि । सद्योजाताय वै नमः नमः । भवेभवे [माम्] न [भवस्व], अतिभवे माम् भवस्व । भवोद्भवाय नमः ।
syntax: A first-person declaration (prapadyāmi), then a nominal sentence of homage with the dative (sadyojātāya … namaḥ), then a request in the imperative (bhavasva mām) set between two locatives, bhave bhave and atibhave, with na. The commentators construe na with the first locative — not in birth after birth, but beyond birth — supplying the verb twice. The last line repeats the homage with a new epithet.

ambiguities.note: Read as written, na stands before atibhave. All three commentators move it to bhave bhave: ‘do not [bring] me to birth after birth, [bring] me to what is beyond birth’. The anonymous commentator: «भवे भवे तत्तज्जन्मनिर्मितं मां न भवस्व न प्रेरयेत्यर्थः».
The base reads bhavasva and the anonymous commentator explains that reading; Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara comment on bhajasva (‘resort to me’, ‘take me up’). The sense of the request is the same.

metre.name: mixed
metre.note: Bhāskara: «सद्योजातम् इति परोष्णिक् त्रिपदा मामन्ता» — three pādas up to mām, in the paroṣṇik metre, and the rest a yajus. As printed the lines count 18, 12 and 7 syllables; with the single namaḥ of Sāyaṇa’s text the first line would have 16.

beginner: This short mantra is the first of five that address five forms, or ‘faces’, of Śiva, each looking in a different direction; together they are called the five ‘brahma’ mantras. This one names Sadyojāta, ‘the one born at once’, whom the old commentators identify with the western face. The speaker says ‘I take refuge’ and bows twice. Then comes the request: not to be kept going from one birth to the next, but to be led beyond birth altogether. The last line bows to Śiva as the one who lifts people out of ‘becoming’ — the cycle of being born again. The commentators read it as a prayer for the knowledge that ends that cycle. The same five mantras open many forms of Śiva worship.
analogy: Like asking a ferryman not for another lap around the lake but to take you across to the far shore.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: The speaker takes refuge in Sadyojāta and offers homage, asks not to be kept in birth after birth but to be brought beyond it, and bows to the one who lifts out of becoming.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa place the mantra among the five that describe the five faces of Mahādeva, and this one as the western face. Sāyaṇa: «मेधाविनः पुरुषस्य ज्ञानोत्पादनाय महादेवसंबन्धिषु पञ्चवक्त्रेषु मध्ये पश्चिमवक्त्रप्रतिपादकं मन्त्रमाह». Bhāskara explains the name: the one who appears in the very moment the god wishes to create, the cause of the world’s unfolding: «सद्योजातं यत्क्षणे सिसृक्षा देवस्य तदानीमेवाविर्भूतं प्रपञ्चोन्मेषहेतुं देवं त्वां प्रपद्यामि».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: All three read the request as release from rebirth. Sāyaṇa: «तत्तज्जन्मनिमित्तं मां न भजस्व न प्रेरयेत्यर्थः», and then «अतिभवे जन्मातिलङ्घननिमित्तं भजस्व तत्त्वज्ञानाय प्रेरय» — impel me toward the knowledge of reality, for passing beyond birth. The anonymous commentator gives the same explanation on the reading bhavasva.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The commentators differ on the person meant. Sāyaṇa: for the person of intelligence, «मेधाविनः पुरुषस्य ज्ञानोत्पादनाय». The anonymous commentator says it is for the three twice-born classes entitled to the śāstra, «त्रैवर्णिकानां शास्त्राधिकारिणां ज्ञानोत्पादनाय»; that restriction is his, and the text itself names no one.

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Bhāskara introduces this anuvāka and the next four together: «अथ पञ्चब्रह्माख्याः पञ्चानुवाका ईश्वराराधनादिषु उपासनादिषु च विनियुक्ताः» — five anuvākas called the five brahmas, used in the worship of the Lord and in meditation. He calls them the five faces of the Lord whose body is all knowledge: «सर्वविद्यादेहस्य सद्योजातादिनामानि पञ्चविद्यास्त्रोतःप्रवर्तकतदीयपञ्चमुखभूतानि पञ्चब्रह्माणि».

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Two differences from the commentators’ texts: bhavasva for bhajasva, and namo namaḥ where Sāyaṇa’s text has a single namaḥ. The Ānandāśrama print of the 80-anuvāka text sets this mantra inside its commentary rather than as a separate line; the sources page lists it as a place to verify.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this text is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The three commentaries present — the anonymous bhāṣya, Sāyaṇa and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara — read the mantra as worship of Śiva’s five faces and a prayer for release; they differ on whom it is for and on the reading bhavasva or bhajasva, not on doctrine.

contemporary.text: The request is not for a better turn of the wheel but for leaving the wheel. Many people know the difference between wanting more of the same and wanting to be done with a pattern altogether. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: What is the difference between asking for a better version of something and asking to be free of it?
reflect.deeper: The commentators move na to ‘birth after birth’. How does the sense change if it stays where it is written?
reflect.practice: Notice one repeated pattern in your day, and ask whether you want it improved or ended.

references.text: Sāyaṇa (his anuvāka 43), Bhāskara (his anuvāka 43) and the anonymous commentator each treat this as the first of the five pañca-brahma anuvākas (10.17–10.21 here).

flags.note: bhavasva (base) against bhajasva in the texts Sāyaṇa and Bhāskara comment on; namo namaḥ (base) against a single namaḥ in Sāyaṇa’s text.
The sources page lists this mantra as missing from the Ānandāśrama pariśiṣṭa text, which prints it within its commentary; to verify against the printed book.
All commentators construe na with bhave bhave, not with atibhave as it stands.
